Prevention: Avoid movement of planting materials (cocoa seedlings, plantain suckers, cocoyam corms) from infected to non- infected areas.
Remove infected pods and cherelles (young pods) and control stem cankers.
Infected pods and husks should be removed and burnt or sprayed fungicides (see yellow control column).
Moist conditions favour the development of this disease so reduce humidity and improve air circulation:
Plant or thin out to the recommended spacing 3 x 3 m for
March/April, clear weeds 3-4 times a year and reduce shade trees to 5-8 per acre.
Ensure there is good drainage and avoid stagnant water.
Monitoring: Monitor cocoa farms at the onset of the rains for the first signs of the disease.
This disease can affect the whole plant but losses to the pods is the most important.
Look out for small brown spots on the surface of the pods which become darker and expand rapidly.
After 3-5 days a white bloom of spores appears on the lession.
The whole surface of the pod can become black after 7-14 days.
When there are cherelles and pods on the trees and the first symptoms of the disease are seen, start direct controls.
If applying fungicide, spot spraying can be carried out but if symptoms are widespread the whole field can be sprayed.
Direct Control: Remove all infected and mummified pods during harvest or preferably as soon as seen, collect the diseased pods and destroy by burning or spray with recommended fungicides.
Harvest frequently, at least monthly so diseased pods are removed from the trees.
Restrictions: When using a pesticide or botanical, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label.
Do not use chemicals with the same mode of action year after year as this can lead to resistance.
